assessment.rationale: Held as a known answer. The end goal as stated, older adults regaining strength, is already achieved by an openly published, freely available intervention: the Cochrane review of progressive resistance strength training pooled 121 randomised trials and about 6,700 older participants and found a large effect on muscle strength (73 trials, SMD 0.84) with small but significant gains in physical ability, chair-rising and stair-climbing, and rare serious adverse events (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD002759.progressive-resistance-strength-training-improving-physical-function-older-adults). The protocol is public, costs nothing and needs no new discovery, so a project whose KPI is 1,000,000,000 older adults regaining strength is a delivery and adherence programme rather than a problem without a discoverable solution. The pharmacological half of the title is genuinely unsolved and should be stated: no drug is approved for sarcopenia, a 2024 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials found bimagrumab increased thigh muscle volume and fat-free mass with no reliable gain in strength, gait speed or six-minute walk distance (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11385021/), its tirzepatide combination was terminated in September 2025, apitegromab preserved muscle during weight loss in 102 adults without proving greater strength or function, and the registry shows only small phase 1-2 drug studies (https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.cond=sarcopenia&query.intr=drug&filter.overallStatus=COMPLETED&pageSize=15). Honest limit: a reframed project on a scalable therapy for people who cannot train, with function rather than mass as the endpoint, would be open work and would need its own prior-art basis; this one, as written, is not opened as new work.

additionalSearches.query: progressive resistance training older adults sarcopenia Cochrane review strength gains evidence
additionalSearches.finding: Cochrane review CD002759 (Liu and Latham) pooled 121 randomised trials and about 6,700 older adults: large effect on strength (73 trials, SMD 0.84), small significant effect on physical ability (33 trials, SMD 0.14), gait speed about +0.08 m/s, rare serious adverse events. An open, free, published answer to older adults regaining strength; durability beyond the trials is not established.

additionalSearches.query: bimagrumab apitegromab sarcopenia drug trial muscle mass function 2026
additionalSearches.finding: A 2024 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials found bimagrumab increased thigh muscle volume and fat-free mass but gave no significant improvement in muscle strength or physical performance (gait speed, six-minute walk) except in the slowest participants. The tirzepatide combination trial was terminated in September 2025; apitegromab preserved muscle in 102 adults losing weight without proven function gains; neither is approved for sarcopenia.

additionalSearches.query: completed drug trials for sarcopenia on ClinicalTrials.gov
additionalSearches.finding: The registry's completed sarcopenia drug studies are small and early: MK-0773 (170, phase 2), MK-677 (72, phase 1-2), intranasal oxytocin (23), metformin (120, phase 1-2), testosterone and thyroid hormone studies. No late-phase trial of a drug approved for sarcopenia appears, confirming no licensed pharmacological answer.

additionalSearches.query: open-source repositories for sarcopenia and muscle aging interventions
additionalSearches.finding: The GitHub search returns only prediction, measurement and analysis projects (sarcopenia risk models, CT psoas radiomics, an offline habit tracker), none a deployed intervention. The open solution for this project is the published exercise prescription, not software.
